title: Phases and Classification of Matter
lead: Matter is anything that occupies space and has mass, and it is met on earth as a solid, a liquid, a gas, or, at high temperatures, a plasma. This section separates mass from weight, states the law that the total quantity of matter does not change when matter changes form, and sorts every sample of matter into an element, a compound, a homogeneous mixture, or a heterogeneous mixture, with the atoms and molecules that all of them are made of.
objectives: Describe the basic properties of each physical state of matter: solid, liquid, and gas
Apply the law of conservation of matter
Classify matter as an element, compound, homogeneous mixture, or heterogeneous mixture with regard to its physical state and composition
Define and give examples of atoms and molecules
summary_html: Matter is anything that occupies space and has mass. The basic building block of matter is the atom, the smallest unit of an element that can enter into combinations with atoms of the same or other elements. In many substances, atoms are combined into molecules. On earth, matter commonly exists in three states: solids, of fixed shape and volume; liquids, of variable shape but fixed volume; and gases, of variable shape and volume. Under high-temperature conditions, matter also can exist as a plasma. Most matter is a mixture: It is composed of two or more types of matter that can be present in varying amounts and can be separated by physical means. Heterogeneous mixtures vary in composition from point to point; homogeneous mixtures have the same composition from point to point. Pure substances consist of only one type of matter. A pure substance can be an element, which consists of only one type of atom and cannot be broken down by a chemical change, or a compound, which consists of two or more types of atoms.

figures.original_caption: The three most common states or phases of matter are solid, liquid, and gas.

(a) The mass of beer precursor materials is the same as the mass of beer produced: Sugar has become alcohol and carbon dioxide. (b) The mass of the lead, lead oxide, and sulfuric acid consumed by the production of electricity is exactly equal to the mass of lead sulfate and water that is formed.
Depending on its properties, a given substance can be classified as a homogeneous mixture, a heterogeneous mixture, a compound, or an element.

The elements hydrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, and sulfur form molecules consisting of two or more atoms of the same element. The compounds water, carbon dioxide, and glucose consist of combinations of atoms of different elements.

The decomposition of water is shown at the macroscopic, microscopic, and symbolic levels. The battery provides an electric current (microscopic) that decomposes water. At the macroscopic level, the liquid separates into the gases hydrogen (on the left) and oxygen (on the right). Symbolically, this change is presented by showing how liquid H₂O separates into H₂ and O₂ gases.
A fuel cell generates electrical energy from hydrogen and oxygen via an electrochemical process and produces only water as the waste product.

exercises.prompt: Why is an object’s mass, rather than its weight, used to indicate the amount of matter it contains?

answer.solution: The mass of an object is a measure of the amount of matter in it, and it does not change when the object is moved. Weight is the force that gravity exerts on the object; it is proportional to the mass, but it changes as the force of gravity changes, so the same object weighs one-sixth as much on the moon as on the earth while containing exactly the same matter. A quantity that changes with location cannot indicate how much matter is present, and a quantity that does not change can.

exercises.prompt: What properties distinguish solids from liquids? Liquids from gases? Solids from gases?

answer.solution: Liquids can change their shape (flow); solids can’t. Gases can undergo large volume changes as pressure changes; liquids do not. Gases flow and change volume; solids do not.

exercises.prompt: How does a heterogeneous mixture differ from a homogeneous mixture? How are they similar?

answer.solution: Both are mixtures: each is composed of two or more types of matter that can be present in varying amounts and can be separated by physical changes. They differ in how the composition is distributed. A heterogeneous mixture has a composition that varies from point to point, so one drop of Italian dressing may be mostly vinegar and another mostly oil; a homogeneous mixture, also called a solution, has a uniform composition and appears visually the same throughout, so every drop of a sports drink tastes the same.

exercises.prompt: How does a homogeneous mixture differ from a pure substance? How are they similar?

answer.solution: The mixture can have a variety of compositions; a pure substance has a definite composition. Both have the same composition from point to point.

exercises.prompt: How does an element differ from a compound? How are they similar?

answer.solution: Both are pure substances, so every sample of either has exactly the same makeup and properties. An element cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical changes, and it consists of a single type of atom. A compound is comprised of two or more elements and can be broken down by chemical changes to yield elements or other compounds, as mercury(II) oxide yields mercury and oxygen when heated. The properties of the combined elements in a compound are different from their properties in the free state.

exercises.prompt: How do molecules of elements and molecules of compounds differ? In what ways are they similar?

answer.solution: Molecules of elements contain only one type of atom; molecules of compounds contain two or more types of atoms. They are similar in that both are comprised of two or more atoms chemically bonded together.

exercises.prompt: How does an atom differ from a molecule? In what ways are they similar?

answer.solution: An atom is the smallest particle of an element that has the properties of that element and can enter into a chemical combination; a molecule consists of two or more atoms joined by strong forces called chemical bonds, and its atoms move around as a unit. So an atom is a single particle, and a molecule is a bonded group of them, which may be atoms of one element, as in hydrogen or sulfur, or of different elements, as in water. Both are incredibly small and light, and both are the units of which matter is made.

exercises.prompt: Many of the items you purchase are mixtures of pure compounds. Select three of these commercial products and prepare a list of the ingredients that are pure compounds.

answer.solution: Answers will vary. Sample answer: Gatorade contains water, sugar, dextrose, citric acid, salt, sodium chloride, monopotassium phosphate, and sucrose acetate isobutyrate.

exercises.prompt:
Classify each of the following as an element, a compound, or a mixture:
(a) copper
(b) water
(c) nitrogen
(d) sulfur
(e) air
(f) sucrose
(g) a substance composed of molecules each of which contains two iodine atoms
(h) gasoline

answer.solution: Take each substance down the two questions of Figure 1.11. Ask first whether it has a constant composition: a substance that can be made in varying proportions and separated by physical means is a mixture, and the section names air and gasoline among its examples of homogeneous mixtures. A pure substance is an element if it cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical changes and consists of one kind of atom, and a compound if it is comprised of two or more elements. Copper, nitrogen, and sulfur appear in the section’s lists of elements, water and sucrose in its discussion of compounds, and a molecule made only of iodine atoms is a molecule of an element, as the hydrogen and oxygen molecules of Figure 1.14 are.

exercises.prompt:
Classify each of the following as an element, a compound, or a mixture:
(a) iron
(b) oxygen
(c) mercury oxide
(d) pancake syrup
(e) carbon dioxide
(f) a substance composed of molecules each of which contains one hydrogen atom and one chlorine atom
(g) baking soda
(h) baking powder

answer.solution: (a) element; (b) element; (c) compound; (d) mixture; (e) compound; (f) compound; (g) compound; (h) mixture

exercises.prompt: A sulfur atom and a sulfur molecule are not identical. What is the difference?

answer.solution: A sulfur atom is the smallest particle of the element sulfur that has the properties of sulfur and can enter into a chemical combination. The section says that one form of the element sulfur consists of units composed of eight sulfur atoms joined by chemical bonds; such a unit is a sulfur molecule, and its eight atoms move around together, much like the cans of soda in a six-pack. The molecule is therefore a bonded group of atoms, and the atom is one member of it.

exercises.prompt: How are the molecules in oxygen gas, the molecules in hydrogen gas, and water molecules similar? How do they differ?

answer.solution: In each case, a molecule consists of two or more combined atoms. They differ in that the types of atoms change from one substance to the next.

exercises.prompt: Why are astronauts in space said to be “weightless,” but not “massless”?

answer.solution: Weight is the force that gravity exerts on an object, and an astronaut in space experiences negligible external forces, gravitational or any other, so she feels weightless. Mass is a measure of the amount of matter in an object, and the amount of matter in the astronaut is the same in space as on the earth, so she is never massless. The section makes the same point about the moon, where her weight is one-sixth of its value on the earth while her mass is unchanged.

exercises.prompt: Prepare a list of the principal chemicals consumed and produced during the operation of an automobile.

answer.solution: Gasoline (a mixture of compounds), oxygen, and to a lesser extent, nitrogen are consumed. Carbon dioxide and water are the principal products. Carbon monoxide and nitrogen oxides are produced in lesser amounts.

exercises.prompt: Matter is everywhere around us. Make a list by name of fifteen different kinds of matter that you encounter every day. Your list should include (and label at least one example of each) the following: a solid, a liquid, a gas, an element, a compound, a homogenous mixture, a heterogeneous mixture, and a pure substance.

answer.solution: Begin with the states, which are the easiest to see: anything rigid with a definite shape is a solid, anything that flows and takes the shape of its container but keeps its volume is a liquid, and anything that fills whatever holds it is a gas. Then classify each item by composition with the questions of Figure 1.11. A substance of constant composition is a pure substance, and it is an element if it consists of one kind of atom, such as the copper of a wire or the aluminum of a can, and a compound if it is made of two or more elements, such as water or table salt. A substance whose composition can vary is a mixture, homogeneous if it is the same throughout, as air, a sports drink, and maple syrup are, and heterogeneous if it varies from point to point, as salad dressing, granite, and a chocolate chip cookie do. One item can carry more than one label, since water is at once a liquid, a compound, and a pure substance.

exercises.prompt: When elemental iron corrodes it combines with oxygen in the air to ultimately form red brown iron(III) oxide called rust. (a) If a shiny iron nail with an initial mass of 23.2 g is weighed after being coated in a layer of rust, would you expect the mass to have increased, decreased, or remained the same? Explain. (b) If the mass of the iron nail increases to 24.1 g, what mass of oxygen combined with the iron?

answer.hint: The matter of the rusted nail is the matter of the iron nail together with the oxygen that combined with it, so the difference between the two masses is the mass of that oxygen.
answer.solution: (a) Increased as it would have combined with oxygen in the air thus increasing the amount of matter and therefore the mass. (b) 0.9 g

exercises.prompt:
As stated in the text, convincing examples that demonstrate the law of conservation of matter outside of the laboratory are few and far between. Indicate whether the mass would increase, decrease, or stay the same for the following scenarios where chemical reactions take place:
(a) Exactly one pound of bread dough is placed in a baking tin. The dough is cooked in an oven at 350 °F releasing a wonderful aroma of freshly baked bread during the cooking process. Is the mass of the baked loaf less than, greater than, or the same as the one pound of original dough? Explain.
(b) When magnesium burns in air a white flaky ash of magnesium oxide is produced. Is the mass of magnesium oxide less than, greater than, or the same as the original piece of magnesium? Explain.
(c) Antoine Lavoisier, the French scientist credited with first stating the law of conservation of matter, heated a mixture of tin and air in a sealed flask to produce tin oxide. Did the mass of the sealed flask and contents decrease, increase, or remain the same after the heating?

answer.solution: The law says that the total quantity of matter does not change when matter converts from one type to another, so in each case ask what was weighed before and what is weighed after, and whether any matter came in or went out between the two weighings. The aroma of baking bread is matter leaving the loaf as gases, along with the water that steams off, and none of it is on the balance afterward. Magnesium burning in air combines with oxygen that was not part of the piece of magnesium, so the ash carries matter that was not weighed at the start. A sealed flask lets nothing in and nothing out, so everything that was weighed before the heating is still inside afterward, whatever it has turned into; that is why Lavoisier’s sealed flask was convincing where an open oven is not.

exercises.prompt:
Yeast converts glucose to ethanol and carbon dioxide during anaerobic fermentation as depicted in the simple chemical equation here:
$$\text{glucose}\;\longrightarrow\;\text{ethanol}+\text{carbon dioxide}$$
(a) If 200.0 g of glucose is fully converted, what will be the total mass of ethanol and carbon dioxide produced?
(b) If the fermentation is carried out in an open container, would you expect the mass of the container and contents after fermentation to be less than, greater than, or the same as the mass of the container and contents before fermentation? Explain.
(c) If 97.7 g of carbon dioxide is produced, what mass of ethanol is produced?

parts.hint: No matter is lost in the conversion, so the products together have the mass of the glucose that became them.
The ethanol and the carbon dioxide together account for all 200.0 g of glucose, so the ethanol is what is left once the carbon dioxide is taken away.

answer.solution: (a) 200.0 g; (b) The mass of the container and contents would decrease as carbon dioxide is a gaseous product and would leave the container. (c) 102.3 g
